title: Basic Story

jokes.text: Long, quiet lull. Don't like it. / It's called contentment.
jokes.setup: The study group notices an unusual quiet moment with no crisis at Greendale.
jokes.punchline: Jeff names the unfamiliar sensation as 'contentment,' as if it's a foreign concept to them.
jokes.explanation: Clean, economic joke that sets up the episode's central theme. The group's unfamiliarity with peace is a smart character observation, and the word 'contentment' delivered as a clinical diagnosis is funny. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, it's weird. Everything's actually going okay right now. Nobody's fighting, nobody's failing a class, there's no elaborate scheme blowing up in our faces.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I know what you mean. It's strange.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's contentment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Contentment? Is that what this is? I forgot what it felt like.

jokes.text: I've got a problem. I don't like Abed's problem with our lack of problems.
jokes.setup: Someone says 'Someone's always got a problem' as a lament about Greendale's chaos.
jokes.punchline: Britta immediately demonstrates the point by manufacturing a meta-problem about Abed's problem-having.
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant — Britta is the living proof of the statement she's responding to. The recursive loop of problem-having is well-constructed and characteristically Britta. The self-awareness without being too winking makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, I just realized I'm commenting on your meta-commentary about me commenting on your meta-commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm out-meta'd the meta character. I'm the meta now.

jokes.text: I commented on his commentary. I just drew a circle around Abed, baby.
jokes.setup: Britta realizes she's done exactly what Abed does — commented on the group's narrative patterns.
jokes.punchline: She triumphantly declares she 'drew a circle around Abed' as if this is a victory, missing that she's also done the same thing.
jokes.explanation: Very character-specific to Britta — she's proud of out-meta-ing Abed while actually demonstrating she's become him. 'Drew a circle around Abed, baby' is a quotable phrase. The irony that she's also now inside the circle is implicit and smart.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm not a gimmick. I'm a person who happens to reference pop culture and watch a lot of TV.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Abed, you literally just described a gimmick.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Fine. But so does everyone else here. Britta's the neurotic one, Troy's the innocent one, Annie's the overachiever, Shirley's the mom, Pierce is the old guy—

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Hey!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: —and Jeff, you're the handsome one who coasts on his looks.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not a gimmick, that's just who I am.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: "I don't think it's nice to pigeonhole people's gimmicks." "You hear me, Two-Voice?"
jokes.setup: Abed is reading from what appears to be a script or book that narrates what's happening to the group in real time.
jokes.punchline: The book apparently calls out Britta as 'Two-Voice,' a dismissive label for her meta-commentary, further layering the self-reference.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed move — narrating the group via external text. 'Two-Voice' as a reductive label for Britta's meta-commentary is a clever insult. The joke is dense and may require multiple viewings to fully land, which is a Community signature.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Hey, nice voice.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: Thanks!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's like you're a person, except you're just a voice.

jokes.text: Dean accidentally presses the PA button, holds an impromptu check-in with the whole school: 'How are you?' / 'Fine.' / 'That's nice. I'm good too. I love you guys.' / 'We love you too.'
jokes.setup: The Dean announces he pressed the PA button on accident but decides to use it anyway.
jokes.punchline: The school collectively participates in this sincere, wholesome, completely absurd communal check-in as if it's perfectly normal.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's warmest and funniest moments. It works on multiple levels: it's absurd (the whole school spontaneously responds in unison), it's character-perfect for the Dean's needy-earnest personality, and it's genuinely sweet. The long timestamp gap before this scene suggests it's played as a full comedic beat. The 'I love you guys' / 'We love you too' exchange is pure Community — the school as a dysfunctional family that works.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Attention students, this is Dean Pelton. I accidentally hit the PA button, but since I have your attention, let me tell you about some exciting campus initiatives.

jokes.text: Your ass is getting appraised, insurance-style.
jokes.setup: School board members deliver news about an insurance appraiser coming.
jokes.punchline: One of them adds an unnecessary, faux-menacing flourish: 'insurance-style.'
jokes.explanation: The school board guys are running gag characters defined by their cheerful obliviousness. 'Insurance-style' as a tough-sounding modifier on something completely mundane is a good bit. Functional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Can you help me find information about this topic?

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Well, information exists, and this topic is definitely a thing that people talk about. You're welcome.

jokes.text: Hey, how hilarious would that be? / Are you guys drunk? / Good luck proving it before we're not.
jokes.setup: School board members are excited about good news in a suspiciously giddy way.
jokes.punchline: 'Good luck proving it before we're not' — an admission of guilt framed as a legal challenge, perfectly capturing their buffoonery.
jokes.explanation: Very economical joke. The phrasing 'good luck proving it before we're not' is a clever construction — it's both an admission and a dare, delivered with complete confidence. The school board characters' casual corruption is a running gag that pays off consistently.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member
dialogue.line: The insurance appraisal process involves a thorough examination of the property. We need to inspect every inch, run our hands along the surfaces, check all the tight spots, and make sure everything is properly... positioned.

jokes.text: Pa-pa-papaya. / Mango. / Strawberry. / Too ripe. / You've been doing this for 30 minutes. / So what? I made all the vegetables disappear.
jokes.setup: Two characters are playing what turns out to be a fruit-matching game on a device.
jokes.punchline: 'I made all the vegetables disappear' — a proud announcement that reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of the game (the items are fruits, not vegetables), suggesting the character has been playing wrong for 30 minutes.
jokes.explanation: Pleasant absurdist bit. The 30-minute time commitment plus the wrong-category taxonomy mistake layers nicely. The reveal that it's irrigation software adds a third beat that elevates the whole sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, did you just admit to that?

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member
dialogue.line: Yes, but my lawyer says I can't be prosecuted because technically I was acting in my capacity as a school board member at the time.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not how the law works.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member
dialogue.line: Isn't it though?

jokes.text: Best $199 I've ever spent. / It's 3 dollars. / What are you playing? / That's control software for some kind of irrigation equipment.
jokes.setup: Character brags about how much they spent on what they think is a game.
jokes.punchline: It's $3. And then a further reveal: it's not a game at all — it's irrigation control software.
jokes.explanation: Double-layered punchline structure — the first (price correction) undercuts the bragging, the second (it's industrial software) reframes the entire bit. Good economy and a satisfying escalation. The comedic gap between $199 and $3 is funny on its own, but the irrigation twist makes it memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. This banana isn't ripe enough. Look at the color — it's still too green. These virtual bananas need to be a deeper yellow.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Britta, it's a video game.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I don't care. Standards are standards.

jokes.text: Something that sounds normal and boring but is scary. Like a raised mole or a turkey deep fryer.
jokes.setup: Someone asks what an insurance appraiser is.
jokes.punchline: Jeff defines it not by function but by emotional register: scary things with mundane presentations, citing a raised mole and a turkey deep fryer as comparators.
jokes.explanation: Smart observational joke. The pairing of 'raised mole' and 'turkey deep fryer' is unexpected but lands as genuinely funny — both are things that look harmless until you think about them. The list construction (two items, specific and mismatched) is classic comedy economy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I spent $199 on entertainment.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: What did you buy?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It's $3 irrigation software. We're playing it like a game.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You spent $199 on $3 software?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: In-app purchases.

jokes.text: Only one man qualified to appraise insurance, and he died 2000 years ago on a cross.
jokes.setup: The group is panicking about the insurance appraiser.
jokes.punchline: Someone claims the only qualified insurance appraiser was Jesus Christ.
jokes.explanation: Solid absurdist joke that earns its laugh from the gap between the mundane subject (insurance appraisal) and the grandiose claim (Jesus). The 'died on a cross' specification adds texture. Not transcendent but reliably funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We have a crisis on our hands.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's the inciting incident.

jokes.text: I've seen insurance appraisers bleed. Their blood's different, darker.
jokes.setup: The group is catastrophizing about the insurance appraiser.
jokes.punchline: Chang claims personal experience seeing their blood and characterizes it as distinctly darker, adding a horror-movie register to bureaucratic anxiety.
jokes.explanation: Very Chang-specific — the claim has the flavor of his deranged over-commitment to bit premises. 'Different, darker' as a way to signal supernatural otherness applied to insurance professionals is a great collision of registers. Character-integrated absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: They're like if a DMV employee and a hitman had a baby. They show up at your door with a clipboard and a smile that says 'I've seen the receipts, and I know what you did.'

jokes.text: You're like Hurricane Katrina dogs that won't let anyone pet them anymore.
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to calm the group down from their reflexive crisis response.
jokes.punchline: He compares them to trauma-damaged rescue dogs from Hurricane Katrina — a surprisingly dark and specific analogy that's both accurate and inappropriate.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The Hurricane Katrina dog metaphor is specific, unexpected, and genuinely insightful about the group's PTSD-like relationship to Greendale crises. It's dark enough to be transgressive but not mean-spirited. The specificity ('won't let anyone pet them anymore') is what elevates it from a good line to a great one — it describes the precise emotional state with unusual precision. Highly quotable, very Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Jesus Christ was an insurance appraiser.

jokes.text: I wrote a paper on those dogs.
jokes.setup: Jeff uses the Hurricane Katrina dog metaphor to describe the group.
jokes.punchline: Britta responds not to the insult but to the subject matter, noting she wrote a paper on those specific dogs — missing (or ignoring) that she's one of them.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback and peak Britta character work. In three words, it accomplishes three things simultaneously: (1) it confirms Jeff's metaphor is accurate because she IS one of those dogs, (2) it shows Britta's reflexive impulse to demonstrate academic credibility, and (3) it completely deflates Jeff's rhetorical moment. The fact that she's academic about the very thing she's accused of being is the precise irony that defines Britta. The economy is exceptional — maximum comedy per word. This is a 8+ joke because it couldn't work for any other character and lands with precision.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Insurance appraisers? They're not like us. They don't have blood like we do. Their blood is different. Colder. They can sense fear.

jokes.text: Pretend we have a renowned Physics Department. / Dean, start learning Swedish.
jokes.setup: Abed proposes an elaborate plan to fool the insurance appraiser involving fake credentials.
jokes.punchline: The plan escalates to the Dean needing to learn Swedish, with no explanation of why this is necessary, followed by 'I'll do my best.'
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed absurdist plan escalation. The Swedish instruction is funny precisely because it's unexplained — the audience's attempt to construct a logic for it is the joke. 'I'll do my best' from the Dean is perfectly obedient and sad.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You guys are like traumatized disaster animals. A fire alarm goes off and you all scatter like you're fleeing a tsunami.

jokes.text: Hickey, you keep in touch with any criminals you busted? / Five. / Get them for costume measurements.
jokes.setup: Abed's plan involves recruiting criminals for costumes to fake a particle accelerator.
jokes.punchline: Hickey answers 'five' with zero context or emotion, as if maintaining contact with exactly five criminals is completely routine for him.
jokes.explanation: Hickey's deadpan 'five' is excellent character economy. The specificity of the number (not 'some,' not 'a few,' but exactly five) and the complete absence of shame or surprise makes this very Hickey. Great economy — the joke is in the one-word answer.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, it's like Hurricane Katrina dogs. They're traumatized, they need time to adjust, they might bite you.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Actually, I've studied post-traumatic stress disorder in canines. The recovery period is typically 18 to 24 months, and aggression is only present in about 12% of cases.

jokes.text: Jeff dragging Abed outside as Abed narrates the meta-structure of his own removal in real time.
jokes.setup: Jeff tells Abed to come outside to talk privately about the story problem.
jokes.punchline: Abed narrates Jeff dragging him 'across a threshold' as a story beat — literally describing his own forced removal as a narrative structural element while it's happening.
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-comedy. The joke is structurally perfect: the act of trying to escape the story IS the story beat Abed is narrating. The 'hero's journey threshold' language applied to being physically dragged outside is very Abed. This is the kind of self-aware comedy Community does uniquely well.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This isn't a story. We're not following some narrative structure.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Jeff, everything is a story. We're always in a story. Even this conversation is a story about a conversation in a story.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not helpful.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No, but it's true. And the fact that you're frustrated proves you know it's true, because in a story, the character always resists the truth right before they accept it.

jokes.text: Jeff's extended speech to Abed about why there is 'no story' — and Abed's clinical observation that Jeff is 'dragging me across a threshold demanding there be no story,' which IS a story.
jokes.setup: Jeff passionately argues there is no story and no crisis and they are not in trouble.
jokes.punchline: The passion and desperation of his 'there is no story' speech is itself a story — Abed identifies this, and Jeff's escalating anxiety confirms it.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sustained comedic ideas. The paradox is elegant: the harder Jeff argues there's no story, the more he creates one. Abed as an impassive narrator of Jeff's obliviousness is perfectly deployed. The structure has the shape of a Catch-22 joke, which is a rare and satisfying form.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Is this a ring? Are you proposing to somebody?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? No! I'm not... that's not... why would you think that?

jokes.text: It's my mom's. I started wearing it because... I don't know, everybody dreams of settling down, right? / And because it fits. She had huge fingers for a woman. / Part of what killed her, really.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals he's been wearing his mother's ring, with an earnest emotional beat about dreaming of settling down.
jokes.punchline: The sentiment is immediately undercut by: (1) the mundane detail that it fits because she had huge fingers, and (2) the darkly casual aside that this was 'part of what killed her, really.'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best dark comedy moment and very Jeff Winger. The structure is excellent: genuine emotional vulnerability → undercut by physical comedy detail (huge fingers) → then a completely unexpected dark aside about mortality that arrives almost as an afterthought. The 'really' at the end is perfect deadpan — as if he's genuinely reasoning through the medical causality in real time. The escalation from sweet to absurd to morbid in rapid succession is very high craft. Genuinely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I wear this ring because it was my mother's. She had large fingers, and that's what killed her.

jokes.text: No, I love Scotch and myself. I tolerate Greendale.
jokes.setup: Someone suggests Jeff loves Greendale.
jokes.punchline: Jeff corrects the hierarchy: Scotch and himself come first, Greendale is merely tolerated.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff deflection joke. The specificity of 'Scotch and myself' (in that order, or is it narcissism first?) is very character-accurate. 'Tolerate' as a word that acknowledges engagement while denying affection is a good word choice. Economical and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This appraisal is going to be completely uneventful.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It'll be like watching Britta and Troy date.

jokes.text: This is going to be the most boring thing to happen here since Britta dated Troy.
jokes.setup: Jeff is reassuring everyone the insurance appraisal won't be a big deal.
jokes.punchline: He cites the Britta/Troy relationship as a known benchmark for maximum Greendale boredom.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to series history (Britta and Troy's low-key relationship). The joke is that by Greendale standards, their romance was notably uneventful — which is itself a critique of their dynamic. Requires some series knowledge to fully land.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Wait, if there's no story, then why am I explaining that there's no story? The fact that I'm explaining it means I'm in a story explaining that there's no story, which means there IS a story.

jokes.text: If there's no story, what am I explaining? I'm in a story. / Okay, think, Abed, think. How do you shake a story? / The answer is in the teacher's lounge.
jokes.setup: Abed realizes his attempt to escape narrative is itself a narrative.
jokes.punchline: He talks himself through the problem out loud like a movie protagonist, then announces with complete confidence that the answer is in the teacher's lounge.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed. The self-narration ('think, Abed, think') as a movie trope playing out in real life is funny, and the declaration about the teacher's lounge is delivered with the confident mystery of a film hero's intuition. The audience doesn't know why the teacher's lounge, and neither does Abed — but the confidence is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ronald Mohammed
dialogue.line: Yes, I know what my name is. Yes, it's real. No, I don't want to hear your jokes about it. And yes, before you ask, my parents hated me.

jokes.text: Hi, my name is Ronald Mohammed. Go ahead, heard them all.
jokes.setup: The insurance appraiser introduces himself.
jokes.punchline: He preemptively acknowledges and dismisses all jokes about his name in one move: 'Go ahead, heard them all.'
jokes.explanation: Very economical character establishment joke. 'Go ahead, heard them all' in a weary deadpan tells us everything about this person's life experience with his name while also being a meta-comment on the kind of joke the audience might be expecting. Subverts the name-joke format by making the character's awareness of it the joke instead.

dialogue.speaker: Ronald Mohammed
dialogue.line: According to section 4, subsection B of the university liability code, a 'dog' is defined as any mammal weighing over 2 pounds that has been on campus for more than 24 consecutive hours.

dialogue.speaker: Ronald Mohammed
dialogue.line: Which technically means... you're all dogs.

jokes.text: But the city defines a dog as any living entity with four legs and a tail. So raccoons, bears, mountain lions, mice — these are all just different sizes of dog.
jokes.setup: Ronald Mohammed continues his bureaucratic definitions.
jokes.punchline: The city's official definition of 'dog' is so broad that raccoons, bears, mountain lions, and mice are all legally just different dog sizes.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalating list (raccoon to bear to mountain lion) has perfect comedic escalation, and the unifying reframe ('different sizes of dog') is elegant absurdist logic. It works because the underlying logic is almost coherent — the definition IS technically inclusive — which makes it funnier than pure randomness. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Jeff, you have something in your teeth.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well Dean, you have liquidated horse meat in your chest.

jokes.text: I know how much you feel for the campus, Jeff. How much you feel in general. And I know you think it's a weakness, but believe me, it's your strength.
jokes.setup: Annie tells Jeff he has 'something in his chest' — emotional investment he denies.
jokes.punchline: The sincerity is played straight, but in context Jeff has just been visibly panicking about the appraisal while claiming he's fine — making Annie's earnest therapeutic insight also a pointed exposure of his hypocrisy.
jokes.explanation: More character drama than pure comedy, but it functions as gentle ironic comedy given Jeff's simultaneous denial of exactly what Annie's describing. Not a strong laugh moment but qualifies as comedic irony.

dialogue.speaker: Ronald Mohammed
dialogue.line: As Camus once said, 'The only way to deal with an unfree world is to become so absolutely free that very existence is an act of rebellion.'

dialogue.speaker: Ronald Mohammed
dialogue.line: Or was that Sartre? No matter. The point is, your claim is denied.

jokes.text: You got something in your teeth. / You got something in your chest.
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to have an emotional moment with Jeff about his feelings.
jokes.punchline: Jeff deflects her emotional insight with a petty physical observation ('you got something in your teeth'), which she immediately mirrors back at him as a metaphor ('you got something in your chest').
jokes.explanation: Structurally very clean. Jeff's deflection is predictably Jeff, but Annie's instant reversal — using the same construction to expose his emotional block — is a sharp comeback that's both funny and character-revealing. The parallel structure ('in your teeth / in your chest') is well-crafted and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm going to break free from narrative structure. No more three-act format, no character arcs, no thematic resolution.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm going to be completely unpredictable and random!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But first, let me explain my motivation in a lengthy monologue that perfectly encapsulates my character journey.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No wait, I'm not doing that. I'm doing the opposite. Everything backwards. Backwards!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I will now speak only in non-sequiturs and absurdist humor to defy conventional comedy structure, which is a clearly established character trait that shows consistent character development.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Why am I still talking about this? I'm overthinking it, which is ironic because I said I wouldn't think about structure, but thinking about not thinking about structure is itself a structure, so—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know what? Forget it. I'm free now.

jokes.text: Four hundred thousand gallons of liquefied horse meat.
jokes.setup: Ronald Mohammed is mid-definition, giving a dry appraisal walkthrough.
jokes.punchline: He announces '400,000 gallons of liquefied horse meat' as a matter-of-fact finding, with zero context or explanation, then continues walking.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional absurdist economy. The joke works entirely because of what's NOT said — no explanation, no reaction, no follow-up. The specificity of '400,000 gallons' and 'liquefied' makes it maximally visual and grotesque in the least amount of words possible. It's a pure absurdist punch delivered with bureaucratic neutrality. This is a 8+ joke because the economy is near-perfect and the specificity does enormous work. One of the most quotable lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I treat reality like an unwanted email subscription. I don't read it, I just delete it and mark it as spam.

jokes.text: And you shall find that salt is the taste of another man's bread, and hard is the way up and down another man's stairs. / Dante. Let's proceed.
jokes.setup: Ronald Mohammed is conducting his appraisal walk-through, apparently quoting something.
jokes.punchline: He cites Dante mid-appraisal and immediately moves on with 'Let's proceed,' treating a medieval literary quotation as standard insurance inspection protocol.
jokes.explanation: Good character bit for Ronald Mohammed — the Dante citation suggests a rich inner life (or bizarre professional training) that's completely at odds with his bureaucratic role. 'Let's proceed' as the transition is perfect deadpan. The appraiser is shaping up to be a great one-episode character.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: So for your final assessment, we're going to need you to demonstrate your understanding of campus safety protocols.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We'll be testing various scenarios, including the vending machine on the third floor. You know, just to see if it can kill you.

jokes.text: No! It's always a story. Everything is a story. Wait, wait — story feeds on conflict. If I stop resisting, it'll stop being a story.
jokes.setup: Abed has been trying to prevent a 'story' from forming all episode.
jokes.punchline: He cracks the code: conflict feeds story, so stopping resistance will end the story — but his excited declaration that he's figured this out is itself conflict and narrative.
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-comedy that works as both comedy and genuine narrative theory. Abed's film-school reasoning applied to real life is very character-specific. The irony that his moment of 'I'll stop creating story' IS the story beat is structurally satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member
dialogue.line: Wait, your name is Dick Appraiser?

dialogue.speaker: Dick Appraiser
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member
dialogue.line: That's got to be the worst name I've ever heard.

jokes.text: Me with a beard? / Keep fighting the story. Keep fighting it until it falls apart. / I'm right. I mean, I'm wrong. I mean, I'm right. I mean, I'm wrong.
jokes.setup: Abed is trying to stop the story by refusing to engage with narrative logic.
jokes.punchline: He imagines himself with a beard as a visual non-sequitur, then spirals into a self-contradicting loop of 'I'm right, I mean I'm wrong' as a way to generate narrative null space.
jokes.explanation: Funny but slightly underbaked. The beard non-sequitur is a good visual gag (inferred), and the right/wrong loop is a nice absurdist spin cycle. The joke is a bit diffuse — it works as a character bit but doesn't have a clean landing.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member
dialogue.line: I'm not the smartest person in the room, I'll admit that. I mean, I only went to Harvard.

jokes.text: Unsubscribe.
jokes.setup: Abed is spiraling through his meta-commentary about stories and narrative.
jokes.punchline: Shirley dismisses the entire conversation with 'Unsubscribe' — internet mailing list language applied to interpersonal exhaustion.
jokes.explanation: One word, maximum impact. 'Unsubscribe' as a reaction to an exhausting conversation is a perfect economy joke. The internet metaphor applied to human interaction is a sharp, modern bit of language comedy. Highly quotable — this is the kind of line that escapes the show and enters common usage. Economy score of 10 because there is literally nothing to cut.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 1
dialogue.line: We should call T.J.Maxx for business advice.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 2
dialogue.line: Hey, there's nothing wrong with my clothes!

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 1
dialogue.line: What? No, the store T.J.Maxx — for business strategies.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 2
dialogue.line: Oh... I thought you were making fun of my outfit.

jokes.text: For the final stage of my appraisal, I'm gonna randomly select one of your vending machines to see if it can be rocked using human strength enough to tip and crush me. In the U.S., each year, six people die this way, and five of them are insurance appraisers, so I take this very seriously.
jokes.setup: Ronald Mohammed announces the final step of the appraisal.
jokes.punchline: He explains the statistic that 5 out of 6 annual vending machine crushing deaths are insurance appraisers — an absurd occupational hazard delivered with complete professional gravitas.
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist joke with strong statistical construction. The joke has perfect structure: the 'six people per year' establishes stakes, the '5 of them are insurance appraisers' subverts expectation with an absurdly specific occupational clustering, and 'so I take this very seriously' is a perfect deadpan capper. The fact that he's about to deliberately attempt this makes it even richer. This is a 8+ joke because the statistical specificity (5 out of 6) is precisely calibrated for maximum absurdity and the character commitment is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 1
dialogue.line: We should call Ben & Jerry's about a business partnership.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 2
dialogue.line: That's a great idea! They could sponsor our events.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 1
dialogue.line: Exactly. I'll reach out to them personally.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 2
dialogue.line: Maybe skip the phone call and just send them an email... from your home address.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 1
dialogue.line: Why would I do that?

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 2
dialogue.line: No reason. Just seems like the professional approach.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 1
dialogue.line: Are you saying I shouldn't call them because of how I look?!

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 2
dialogue.line: What? No! I just—

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member 1
dialogue.line: You think Ben & Jerry are going to judge me for my weight!

jokes.text: No new species have been discovered here in a week.
jokes.setup: Ronald Mohammed is listing the improvements he found at Greendale.
jokes.punchline: He cites 'no new species discovered in a week' as a positive development — implying that new species WERE being regularly discovered before.
jokes.explanation: Excellent deadpan Greendale mythology joke. The fact that this is listed as a POSITIVE improvement implies a previous baseline of regular species discovery. The word 'week' is specifically calibrated — not 'month' or 'year,' suggesting it was happening quite recently and quite often. Very economical delivery of a lot of comedic information.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: More people die from vending machine accidents than from actual accidents. So if Greendale is sold, I'm going to throw myself at a vending machine until it falls on me.

jokes.text: This property has value. / Oh, yeah! Best news ever. [immediately followed by...] That means we can sell it. / We can finally sell it.
jokes.setup: Everyone celebrates when the appraiser declares the school a property asset.
jokes.punchline: The school board immediately reveals they interpret 'value' as 'sell it' — the good news for the school is simultaneously the mechanism of its destruction.
jokes.explanation: Good structural irony — the celebration cut short by the reveal of the board's agenda. The beat between 'Oh, yeah! Best news ever' and 'That means we can sell it' is a tonal whiplash that's both funny and dramatically effective. The timing of the reversal is tight and the audience is ahead of the group.

jokes.text: Press stop on Dave Matthews.
jokes.setup: Jeff interrupts the celebration to respond to the bad news.
jokes.punchline: He tells someone to stop the Dave Matthews (celebratory music playing), using the band choice as a character-specific cultural shorthand for a certain kind of hollow triumphalism.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's cultural snobbery deployed well. 'Dave Matthews' as a shorthand for a specific kind of white-guy celebration is a solid observational reference. Good economy and character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I came here today to say goodbye, to reflect on my time at Greendale, to inspire you all with words of wisdom and—

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: You know what? I have no idea what I'm doing. I never have. I'm just a man in a suit making it up as I go along, hoping no one notices.

jokes.text: Maybe we're not as smart as you. I mean, we only went to Yale.
jokes.setup: Jeff/group pushes back on the school board's plan to sell Greendale.
jokes.punchline: School board member performs false modesty ('maybe we're not as smart as you') immediately undercut by credentialist one-upmanship ('we only went to Yale').
jokes.explanation: Classic false-modesty-reveal structure executed cleanly. The 'we only went to Yale' as a humblebrag delivered with apparent obliviousness is consistent with the school board characters' comic DNA. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I can't promote the save campaign. My Twitter is just atheistic rants and meal photos.

jokes.text: We should call T.J. Maxx right away. / Dude, I told you. This jacket looks fine. / No, to talk about selling this place.
jokes.setup: School board member brings up T.J. Maxx as a potential buyer.
jokes.punchline: His partner thinks it's about his jacket — which suggests he's self-conscious about wearing discount clothing — before the clarification reveals the actual meaning.
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection with an extra layer: the clarification reveals that the partner IS apparently sensitive about the jacket, suggesting it's a real ongoing insecurity between them. The double meaning works efficiently and adds texture to their dynamic.

jokes.text: Oh, Richie, you're my friend, but that is the last thing you need. / Tough love received, bro.
jokes.setup: Richie suggests Ben & Jerry's as a buyer.
jokes.punchline: Carl shuts it down as 'the last thing you need' — implying Richie has a weight/diet issue — and Richie's 'tough love received, bro' is an oddly mature acceptance.
jokes.explanation: Good character-building joke for the school board duo. The Ben & Jerry's aside adds a personal dimension to their dynamic. 'Tough love received, bro' is a genuinely funny response — the casual acceptance of a mild body-shaming remark as friendship wisdom is very specific to this kind of bro relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What if there's treasure buried somewhere on campus? We could dig it up and sell it!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, that's... that's not how anything works.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh, so you're saying you've never found treasure before? Well, I have. Twice. Three times if you count that money I found in my couch.

jokes.text: I did it. This school is story-free. We can be content now forever.
jokes.setup: Abed believes he has successfully stopped the narrative by achieving a contentment state.
jokes.punchline: He announces this triumph just as the school is literally about to be sold — the most dramatic story beat of the episode — making his declaration of 'story-free' hilariously, perfectly wrong.
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic payoff to Abed's episode-long meta-arc. His triumphant announcement of 'story-free' arrives at exactly the moment a massive story begins. The structural irony is excellent — it's the narrative equivalent of walking into a wall while saying 'I see clearly now.' The timing is what makes it an 8.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about ways to save Greendale. What if we partnered with a major corporation? A restaurant chain, perhaps?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I mean, I've been working with them for months now. Subway's really committed to supporting educational institutions.

jokes.text: Let me be one of the six this year. / Craig. Craig, this vending machine is not gonna tip over and crush you. / Why not? Why? / Because we fixed it when we saved Greendale.
jokes.setup: The Dean is visibly distressed about the school being sold.
jokes.punchline: He wants to be crushed by the vending machine (from Ronald Mohammed's statistic) — and Jeff's correction ('because we fixed it') is both practical and an inadvertent reminder that saving the school now means they're losing it anyway.
jokes.explanation: Strong callback that builds on the vending machine joke while adding emotional weight. The Dean wanting to be crushed as a grief response is good dark comedy, and Jeff's matter-of-fact response ('we fixed it') lands as both practical and devastating. The irony that fixing the school led to this outcome is embedded in the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That was unexpected.

jokes.text: If I come over there, there are gonna be two sounds: me hitting you twice.
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Chang or Abed) is behaving annoyingly.
jokes.punchline: Hickey's threat is so specific and minimal — 'two sounds: me hitting you twice' — that it's funnier than any elaborate threat. The mathematical reduction of violence to its simplest components.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy joke. The phrasing 'two sounds: me hitting you twice' is brilliantly constructed — the logical equivalence between sounds and hits presented as a threat is both funny and oddly precise. It's completely Hickey: no theatrics, no color, just clinical violence arithmetic. Very quotable. This is an 8+ joke because the construction is genuinely impressive — it couldn't be tighter, and it couldn't belong to any other character.

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member
dialogue.line: I'm very proud of Greendale Community College.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Rep
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: School Board Member
dialogue.line: Well, proud of its potential. The reality is a dumpster fire, but the potential? Chef's kiss.

jokes.text: Hello, Greendale, as you know, our school will soon be replaced by a sandwich university. However, every ending is also a beginning... Okay, okay, I should've written this out. I thought I'd be able to come up with something on the fly.
jokes.setup: The Dean makes a school-wide PA announcement about the school's closure.
jokes.punchline: His inspirational speech immediately collapses because he hadn't prepared it, and he admits this publicly over the PA system to the entire school.
jokes.explanation: Good Dean Pelton character comedy. His aspirational reaches always exceed his grasp, and the public collapse of an inspirational speech is very on-brand. 'I thought I'd be able to come up with something on the fly' as a sincere admission is both sad and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Rep
dialogue.line: It's actually a footlong.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Thanks for ruining my joke with accuracy.

jokes.text: The reason I have 48 followers is that I don't exploit them. They come to me for atheistic rants and photos of my meals, not this obnoxiousness.
jokes.setup: Annie suggests using social media to save Greendale.
jokes.punchline: Britta refuses on principle, citing her 48-follower base who come to her for atheistic rants and food photos — a perfect self-portrait of irrelevant social media presence.
jokes.explanation: Peak Britta character comedy. The specificity of '48 followers' is devastating — not 50, not 100, but 48. And the content (atheistic rants and meal photos) is an exact satirical portrait of a certain type of 2013 social media user. The indignation with which she protects this tiny audience is perfect irony. Very character-specific and very quotable. Close to 8+ territory because of the exceptional character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: So if a footlong is twelve inches, why do you call it a footlong? A foot is twelve inches. That's the definition of a foot.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Rep
dialogue.line: It's just what we call it.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: But that's circular reasoning. The name describes the measurement, but the measurement doesn't match the name. So either the footlong isn't a foot long, or a foot isn't twelve inches, which means every ruler in the world is wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Rep
dialogue.line: Look, I just make sandwiches.

jokes.text: Just ask Chris Brown or China.
jokes.setup: Britta is making the point that internet attention changes things.
jokes.punchline: She cites Chris Brown and China as examples of things the internet has changed — an absurdly mismatched pair united only by negative internet attention.
jokes.explanation: Topical joke that relies on 2013 cultural references without much twist. The pairing is mildly funny (a pop star and a nation), but it's more a quick observational aside than a crafted joke. Ages poorly.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I've organized all the files by color, cross-referenced them by department, and labeled everything with my new label maker.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: It's pathetic hope placed in a simple label maker.

jokes.text: Jeff, you made Annie cry. / Well, if it's any consolation, this is the last time that will ever happen.
jokes.setup: Jeff has dismissed Annie's idea and she cries.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'consolation' is that this is the last time he'll ever make her cry — which sounds like a promise to be kinder, but actually means they're all about to part ways forever.
jokes.explanation: Smart dark joke with emotional undertow. The double meaning is elegant — it sounds like a promise of better behavior but means 'we're all leaving.' Delivers a genuine emotional gut punch alongside the laugh. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Russell Borchert, Russell Borchert, smells like a burned shirt.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Russell Borchert, Russell Borchert, keeps his toys in a locked drawer.

jokes.text: I know how to save Greendale. / Treasure. Buried treasure. / Okay, I'm tapped.
jokes.setup: The group is desperately brainstorming ways to save the school.
jokes.punchline: Someone confidently announces they know how to save Greendale — 'buried treasure' — and Jeff immediately ends the meeting.
jokes.explanation: Solid absurdist moment. The confidence of the 'buried treasure' delivery followed by Jeff's flat 'okay, I'm tapped' is a good two-beat joke. Functions as setup for the later treasure plot payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: You know, it's a shame really. Borchert's actual accomplishments - his groundbreaking work in administration, his innovative approaches to institutional management - all completely overshadowed by this ridiculous sexual legend.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Nobody remembers the real achievements. It's always just the scandals, the rumors, the... the sexual exploits.

jokes.text: Wait! Are we sure we can't stop the school from being sold to Subway? / I'm afraid so, Chang. / Okay, I just wanted to make sure. / Screw you, guys. It's time to get paid.
jokes.setup: Chang asks one last clarifying question before apparently accepting the situation.
jokes.punchline: His 'I just wanted to make sure' followed by immediate pivot to 'Screw you guys, it's time to get paid' reveals his question was due diligence before defecting — not last-minute loyalty.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character jokes. The structure is perfect: a seemingly earnest clarifying question is immediately revealed to be a purely mercenary due-diligence check before betrayal. 'Screw you guys, it's time to get paid' is a highly quotable line and perfectly captures Chang's character — the false attempt at loyalty immediately abandoned. The timing (the pause between 'make sure' and 'screw you guys') is excellent. This is 8+ because it's character-specific, structurally tight, and genuinely very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Rep
dialogue.line: We'd like to offer you a teaching position at Subway University.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Sandwich Law? That's a legitimate academic specialization.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Rep
dialogue.line: It's more of a corporate training program, but sure.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm going to need tenure and a corner office that overlooks the condiment station.

jokes.text: Chang just unexpectedly betrayed the group for the last time.
jokes.setup: Chang defects to Subway's side.
jokes.punchline: Abed narrates the moment as a show beat — but notes it's the 'last time,' acknowledging the series is ending without breaking character.
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta joke. 'For the last time' does double duty: it's Abed commenting on the show's narrative patterns AND acknowledging series finality in-universe. The 'unexpectedly' is ironic since it's very expected from Chang — which is itself the joke. Pure Abed, pure Community.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Rep
dialogue.line: This card gives you lifetime access to Subway.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Rep
dialogue.line: Lifetime. Subway. Access.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Rep
dialogue.line: Do you understand what you're holding?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: A depression?

jokes.text: If you wanna dynamite it, all we ask is that you let us light the fuse. / Yeah, we hate this place.
jokes.setup: The school board is handing Greendale over to Subway.
jokes.punchline: They request to personally light the dynamite — a request that reveals casual institutional hatred of the school they ostensibly govern.
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy from the school board. The cheerful enthusiasm for demolition followed by the matter-of-fact 'yeah, we hate this place' is a funny reveal of their genuine feelings about the institution they run.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie and Abed aren't ready for change. They're millennials.

jokes.text: Proud of its potential. / Love its potential.
jokes.setup: Called out for saying they were proud of a school they just said they hate.
jokes.punchline: They pivot instantly to 'proud of its potential' — the classic corporate reframe — with zero embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: Decent bit on corporate doublespeak. The pivot is quick and clean, but it's a fairly common joke pattern (say the opposite → retract → reframe as 'potential'). Functional but not distinctive.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Do you remember how we first got together? I thought it was something special.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, I wanted to sleep with you.

jokes.text: What, can't wait until Greendale's corpse is cold before you put it on a 6-inch white bun? / Young lady, that's not fair. Subway doesn't call its bread 'buns,' and we don't serve white. We serve Italian, honey oat, nine-grain wheat. / Thanks for making my joke accurate. / Now it's hilarious.
jokes.setup: Annie makes a pointed metaphor about the school being 'put on a 6-inch white bun.'
jokes.punchline: The Subway rep corrects her bread terminology in earnest, which Annie interprets as making her insult MORE accurate — 'Thanks for making my joke accurate.'
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured joke. The Subway rep's earnest brand defense completely misses the rhetorical point and in doing so deepens the insult. Annie's response ('Thanks for making my joke accurate') is sharp and confident. The structure is a classic straight-man-escalation: the pedantic correction makes the punchline land harder. 'Now it's hilarious' as the rep's oblivious self-assessment is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You know, I think we finally really get each other.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, we do.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I mean, we've been through so much together. We really understand each other now.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Absolutely. I feel like we could get each other done.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: ...Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? I meant emotionally understand each other!

jokes.text: What, can't wait until Greendale's corpse is cold before you put it on a 6-inch white bun?
jokes.setup: Subway executives are already moving into the Dean's office
jokes.punchline: Annie mixes corpse imagery with Subway menu specificity — 'corpse... on a 6-inch white bun' — the brand-specific detail making the death metaphor absurdly precise
jokes.explanation: Annie's righteous anger channeled into a genuinely clever food-meets-death metaphor. The specificity of '6-inch white bun' makes the insult funnier because it shows she's done her Subway homework even while furious. Good economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm going to go to the freshman dorm party tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I know I'm way too old for this, but I'm going anyway because I have poor judgment and boundary issues.

jokes.text: Young lady, that's not fair. Subway doesn't call its bread 'buns,' and we don't serve white. We serve Italian, honey oat, nine-grain wheat. / Thanks for making my joke accurate. / Now it's hilarious.
jokes.setup: Annie makes a passionate, angry metaphor involving Subway bread
jokes.punchline: The Subway executive corrects her bread terminology — which Annie immediately weaponizes: 'Thanks for making my joke accurate. Now it's hilarious.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and among the best-structured two-liners. The Subway exec's pedantic brand correction is funny on its own; Annie's immediate reframe — 'Thanks for making my joke accurate' — turns the correction into self-own. 'Now it's hilarious' as a button is perfect. The structure (setup → unexpected correction → reversal of correction into triumph) is textbook misdirection. Earns high scores across structure, economy, and earned-vs-cheap. High quotability — this is a memorable exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We could get married, settle down. You know, wake up together, have coffee on the porch, watch our kids play in the yard.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We'd argue about whose turn it is to take out the recycling. I'd pretend to fix the dishwasher but actually just jiggle the door handle a few times.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We'd watch TV on a Saturday night and fall asleep before 10 PM. You'd gain thirty pounds, I'd lose my hair, and we'd stop having sex but keep doing it anyway because we'd feel obligated.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We'd take one vacation every other year to a place that's not quite what the brochure promised. We'd have one big fight about money in the car ride home, and that would be our lives.

jokes.text: Wait. You don't call your bread 'buns.' What do you call them? / Bread. / Bread is a substance. What do you call the units of bread you use, 'breads'?
jokes.setup: Jeff picks up Annie's bread terminology thread.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's escalating linguistic interrogation — 'bread is a substance, what do you call the units, breads?' — is a sincere philosophical deconstruction of Subway's naming conventions.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that escalates the previous bit. The mass noun vs. count noun argument ('bread is a substance') is genuinely clever linguistic territory for a sitcom to explore. Jeff is exactly the kind of character to pursue this tangent with complete seriousness. The unresolved nature of the question (we don't get an answer) is funny — Subway's answer has broken Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So what are we doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I don't know, what do you want to do?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, I'm thinking we could start with some foreplay, maybe work our way up to—

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Can we customize that? I'd like to substitute the foreplay for direct penetration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Sure. And would you like that with or without eye contact?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Without, please. And can I get the emotional detachment on the side?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Absolutely. Anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yeah, can we make this to go?

jokes.text: I got one of these label things. I mean, it makes custom labels. This was gonna help me get organized.
jokes.setup: The Dean is emotional about losing the school and is trying to show he could have done better.
jokes.punchline: His evidence of potential competence is a label maker — an office supply that implies organization but is so mundane it's pathetic as a symbol of institutional ambition.
jokes.explanation: Good Dean comedy. The label maker as the pinnacle of his administrative aspirations is both sad and funny. 'This was gonna help me get organized' — the 'was gonna' implies it never happened — is a small tragedy perfectly rendered.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone, this is a covert operation. We need complete radio silence. No one can know about this treasure.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I've color-coded the map by risk level. Red zones are off-limits unless we establish a buddy system with hand signals.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We'll rendezvous at 0600 hours. Wear dark clothing, bring a flashlight with a red filter so we don't compromise our night vision, and for God's sake, nobody tells anyone.

jokes.text: Here's our 1987 civil rights march. This was when we started offering Photoshop classes.
jokes.setup: The Dean is showing historic Greendale photos.
jokes.punchline: What was labeled as a civil rights march is revealed (via the Dean's correction) to be a Photoshopped image — Greendale's 'history' is fabricated.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The implication is devastating: Greendale's 1987 civil rights march was a Photoshopped image created to give the school fake historical prestige. The connection between 'started offering Photoshop classes' and the existence of this historical record is an economical, sharp, institution-specific joke. It's dark, original, and says something specific about institutional self-mythology. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: I'm from Greendale.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Greendale? I know Greendale. I dated a girl from there in '82.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Yes, yes, 'More than women's butts or hooters.' Very mature, you two.
jokes.setup: Someone is explaining the legend of Russell Borchert — a computer professor — by reciting a rhyme about his preferences.
jokes.punchline: The Dean dismisses this with exasperated adult condescension ('very mature, you two') while still reciting the rhyme himself.
jokes.explanation: Light character moment. The Dean's faux-prudishness while quoting the crass rhyme is mild irony. Not a strong joke on its own but serves scene context.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Wait, you're from Riverside?

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Born and raised.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: No kidding. My old man used to take me down to the docks there.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: The docks? Ha! I haven't thought about those in years.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Remember that song? The one all the guys used to sing?

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Oh man, yeah! How does it go?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Riverside, riverside, where the whiskey flows free...

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: And the ladies are loose and the nights never freeze!

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: That's it! That's it!

dialogue.speaker: Hickey and Duncan
dialogue.line: Riverside, riverside, home of the brave and the bold...

jokes.text: The truth is, Greendale had a computer professor. By the way, he was a millionaire and a genius. He has sex with one computer, and that's his legacy?
jokes.setup: The legend of Russell Borchert is being discussed — a man remembered for 'making love to a computer and dying of the first computer virus.'
jokes.punchline: The Dean's exasperation that a millionaire genius's legacy is entirely defined by one sexual misadventure is both a defense of Borchert and an implicit observation about how reputation works.
jokes.explanation: Good joke. The Dean's indignant advocacy for Borchert's full legacy is funny, and 'he has sex with one computer' as a diminishing construction is well-phrased. The implication is also slightly sympathetic — the Dean perhaps relates to being defined by a single embarrassing quality.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Remember those nights at Stainsbury Pub? Good times.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: The best. My mother used to work there.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Really? What did she do?

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: She was a prostitute.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that's... that's quite a revelation.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Yeah, she was very popular with the regulars.

jokes.text: So after all my work, how will I be remembered? / The bald dean with glasses, I guess.
jokes.setup: The Dean asks rhetorically how he'll be remembered.
jokes.punchline: Jeff responds with purely physical descriptors — 'the bald dean with glasses' — stripped of any personality or achievement.
jokes.explanation: Understated Jeff brutality. 'The bald dean with glasses' as a complete summation of a person's legacy is a small but effective put-down. The Dean's vulnerability in the question makes the bluntness of the answer land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: My mother's missing a thumb.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: What? Your mother had both her thumbs when I knew her.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: You knew my mother?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Yeah, we dated for a while back in the day.

jokes.text: You aware there's an engraved plate on this, says 'The truth is behind this picture'? / Of course. I'm not an idiot. [pause] Whoa, wait. It meant literally?
jokes.setup: Jeff notices an engraved plate on a picture saying 'the truth is behind this picture,' which the Dean claims to have always known about.
jokes.punchline: The Dean's immediate 'of course I'm not an idiot' followed by his sudden realization ('Whoa, wait. It meant literally?') reveals he'd interpreted it metaphorically for years.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dean Pelton character joke. The structure is perfect: confident assertion of knowledge → pause → revelation of complete misunderstanding. The Dean has presumably looked at that plaque for years and taken it as philosophical wisdom when it was literal instructions. 'It meant literally?' is the perfect horrified realization. This is 8+ because the character integration is exceptional — this exact obliviousness/vanity combo is quintessential Dean Pelton.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Wait, you knew my mother?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Yeah, we go way back.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Well, I guess that makes us family then.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: To family connections... however they happen.

jokes.text: You were teaching Fundamentals of Law? / Yeah. / Think you could make the transition to teaching Sandwich Law? / It's essentially the same, I'm sure, just a bit more focused.
jokes.setup: The Subway rep is talking to Jeff about his teaching role.
jokes.punchline: 'Sandwich Law' as a legal specialty, and the rep's breezy claim that it's 'essentially the same as Fundamentals of Law, just more focused' is corporate doublespeak applied to an absurd subject.
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist corporate comedy. 'Sandwich Law' is a funny concept, and the earnest claim that it's 'essentially the same' as actual law is a good bit of brand obliviousness. The implication that all of Jeff's legal training is applicable to sandwich jurisprudence is quietly insulting.

jokes.text: That's a Subway black card. It entitles you to 5-dollar footlongs for life. / For life, Mr. Winger. For life.
jokes.setup: Jeff is being recruited to teach Sandwich Law at Subway University.
jokes.punchline: The 'black card' as an elite status symbol offers a lifetime supply of... $5 footlongs. The rep's dramatic 'For life, Mr. Winger' treats this as a profound and weighty offer.
jokes.explanation: Good gap-between-register-and-reality joke. The 'For life, Mr. Winger' delivery applied to the offer of cheap sandwiches is funny. The black card as a prestige object offering a $5 value item is a nice corporate satire.

jokes.text: I'm worried about Abed and Annie. They're not ready for this to end. / They're part of the adulthood-begins-at-30 generation.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta discuss how Abed and Annie are handling the school's closure.
jokes.punchline: Britta characterizes their generation as the 'adulthood-begins-at-30' generation — a pointed generational observation delivered by someone who is herself not exactly a paragon of adult maturity.
jokes.explanation: Decent observational joke. The irony that Britta is making this generational distinction while herself being at Greendale at an older age is implicit. The phrase 'adulthood-begins-at-30 generation' is a good cultural shorthand.

jokes.text: Yeah. I mean, it's over, but on the other hand, it's over.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are discussing the end of Greendale — sad but also a relief.
jokes.punchline: Britta acknowledges both sides of the equation but they're the same side: 'it's over' as both the bad news and the good news.
jokes.explanation: Elegant little joke. The parallel construction where both the negative and positive are the same phrase is philosophically funny — it acknowledges ambivalence by collapsing the distinction between good and bad. Very economical.

jokes.text: And to think this all started because you wanted to... / Nail you. / Yeah, I regret nothing.
jokes.setup: Britta begins to get nostalgic about how the whole Greendale journey started.
jokes.punchline: Jeff completes her sentence with 'nail you' — revealing the founding motivation of the entire show was his sexual pursuit of Britta — and says he regrets nothing.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the show's premise. Jeff's crass reduction of the entire community college experience to a failed hookup attempt is very character-consistent. 'I regret nothing' as a sincere declaration after everything they went through is funny and oddly touching.

jokes.text: What did either of us really get done aside from each other? / Exactly. And what are either of us gonna be leaving with?
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are reflecting on their time at Greendale.
jokes.punchline: The double entendre of 'aside from each other' / 'leaving with' is played as genuine retrospective while also being a crass summary of their relationship's transactional nature.
jokes.explanation: Light double entendre that works within the Jeff/Britta scene rhythm. Not a strong standalone joke but functions as comedic texture in an otherwise dramatic conversation.

jokes.text: I should go clean out my locker, she said at the age of 33.
jokes.setup: Britta is wrapping up her Greendale chapter.
jokes.punchline: She narrates her own action in third person with its age context — 'she said at the age of 33' — a moment of wry self-awareness about how odd her life trajectory has been.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Britta moments. The self-narration format 'she said at the age of 33' is unexpected and perfectly captures Britta's occasional flash of genuine self-awareness. It's funny and sad simultaneously, which is the best kind of sitcom comedy. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Let's get married. / What? / Yeah, right? I mean, this is what matters, isn't it?
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie are alone together, emotionally raw about the school closing.
jokes.punchline: Jeff proposes marriage seemingly out of nowhere — presented as a solution to existential uncertainty rather than romantic feeling.
jokes.explanation: More of a dramatic beat with comedic framing. The abruptness of the proposal is funny but also genuine, which creates an interesting tonal ambiguity. Functions as both comedy and character development.

jokes.text: Get a house we can't afford, a dog that makes us angry. Dedicate an entire cabinet to grocery bags. Realise we have a favourite brand of olive oil?
jokes.setup: Jeff is making the case for getting married by listing the hallmarks of adult settled life.
jokes.punchline: His vision of domestic bliss escalates to increasingly mundane and specific details — a dog that 'makes us angry,' the grocery bag cabinet, a favorite olive oil brand — presented as aspirational.
jokes.explanation: Very good observational list joke. The escalation from vaguely aspirational (house, dog) to hyper-specific domestic details (grocery bag cabinet, olive oil brand) is well-paced. 'A dog that makes us angry' is the best item — dogs are supposed to make you happy, so a dog that makes you angry is a specifically defeated kind of domestic dream. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Medium roughness, high tempo? / Let's make it a number eight.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie are about to have sex on the dean's new table.
jokes.punchline: They negotiate the parameters of their encounter with the clinical efficiency of restaurant ordering or workout planning — 'number eight' as a coded preference.
jokes.explanation: Good bit on the clinical efficiency of Jeff and Annie's relationship dynamics. 'Number eight' as a mutually understood shorthand for a specific sexual encounter style is funny — it implies a lengthy and well-cataloged history. The Subway context (number 8 is a Subway sandwich) adds an extra layer of unconscious corporate infiltration.

jokes.text: Buried treasure! Buried treasure! / Lock the doors, close the blinds. / We could save Greendale, Jeff.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie are about to have sex when Abed and Annie burst in with the treasure news.
jokes.punchline: Abed and Annie arrive at exactly the wrong moment, completely oblivious to what they're interrupting, with 'buried treasure' energy that couldn't be more different from the room they've walked into.
jokes.explanation: Good comedic interruption. The contrast between the intimate scene being set up and the childlike 'buried treasure!' energy of the intruders is well-executed. Abed's 'lock the doors, close the blinds' mirrors what Jeff said to Annie for a different reason, adding an extra ironic layer.

jokes.text: Buried treasure, buried treasure, buried treasure. / Interesting. / Emergency meeting.
jokes.setup: Abed and Annie are breathlessly conveying the treasure news.
jokes.punchline: Abed's response to the entire thing — after a beat — is simply 'Interesting,' followed by his declaration of an emergency meeting. The speed from treasure revelation to committee protocol is very Abed.
jokes.explanation: Good Abed character beat. His processing of information through the lens of narrative structure — 'interesting' as a plot assessment, then immediately 'emergency meeting' as his standard response protocol — is very character-consistent. The deadpan of 'interesting' after multiple 'buried treasure' shouts is the joke.

jokes.text: And that's how I ended up at Greendale. / Isn't it strange how it took this school shutting down for you and I to know each other?
jokes.setup: Two background characters are having a surprisingly deep conversation about their time at Greendale.
jokes.punchline: Two completely non-featured characters have a touching moment about connection that mirrors the main characters' emotional arcs — the joke is that this whole conversation is happening with people we've never seen before.
jokes.explanation: Meta joke about background characters having the same emotional experience as the leads. Works as an observational comment on the show's world — Greendale affects everyone, not just the study group. Mild but functional.

jokes.text: Maybe go stay with family in Lincolnshire. / Lincolnshire? / Yeah. / Where in Lincolnshire? / Just a little town called Scunthorpe.
jokes.setup: Two workers are bonding over shared connections to the UK.
jokes.punchline: The town of Scunthorpe — whose name contains a profanity — is introduced with the gravity of a dramatic revelation, setting up a whole sequence.
jokes.explanation: Classic dirty-word-in-place-name joke, which is a well-worn comedic device. The setup is good (the gravity of 'just a little town called...') but the underlying joke type is not very original. Earns its keep as setup for the subsequent song.

jokes.text: O'er the lady's smocks I tarry / Through the hollyhocks and glen / For a piss and a thrush in Scunthorpe / Then it's off to Henningpen
jokes.setup: One worker recognizes Scunthorpe and launches into a traditional-sounding pub song about it.
jokes.punchline: The song is an escalating series of crude double-entendres ('a piss and a thrush') delivered in the style of an earnest folk song, culminating in 'Henningpen' — another suggestive place name.
jokes.explanation: Surprisingly well-executed. The commitment to the folk-song format, the escalating crude imagery disguised as pastoral imagery, and 'Henningpen' as a final reveal all work together. The surprise of a full song being performed by background characters is itself a comedic choice. The double-meaning of 'thrush' (a bird / a yeast infection) in a 'pastoral' song is the kind of layered wordplay Community enjoys.

jokes.text: O'er the lady's smocks I tarry / Through the hollyhocks and glen / For a piss and a thrush in Scunthorpe / Then it's off to Henningpen
jokes.setup: One character mentions Scunthorpe; the other recognizes it and launches into a song
jokes.punchline: The folk song is an extended Scunthorpe double-entendre with added crude language ('for a piss and a thrush') disguised in mock-pastoral verse
jokes.explanation: The folk song is an enjoyable escalation of the Scunthorpe joke. The pastoral verse form around crude content ('for a piss and a thrush') is a reasonable execution of the double-entendre setup. The character integration is weak because these are background characters with no established voice. Mildly funny but not among the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: I lost my virginity at Stainsbury's. / My mother was a Stainsbury whore.
jokes.setup: Both workers discover they know the same pub ('Stainsbury's') in Lincolnshire.
jokes.punchline: The escalating emotional connection peaks with 'My mother was a Stainsbury whore' — a confession that is both bonding and horrifying, delivered with warmth.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest late-game moments. The escalation from 'I lost my virginity there' to 'my mother was a Stainsbury whore' is a perfect dark comedy escalation. The fact that it's said warmly, as a bonding revelation rather than with shame, makes it funnier. Very quotable. The British pub comedy register is well-executed.

jokes.text: Mine was missing a thumb. / Two thumbs, she got both.
jokes.setup: Following 'my mother was a Stainsbury whore,' the other worker reciprocates about his mother.
jokes.punchline: He specifies his mother was 'missing a thumb,' and the other responds with relief/pride that his mother had both thumbs — presented as a distinguishing quality of these two women.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The thumb detail is an extraordinary comedic choice — specific, grotesque, and completely unexpected as the distinguishing characteristic between two Stainsbury pub regulars. 'Two thumbs, she got both' as a proud maternal defense is the perfect response. The economy is near-perfect. This joke works because of the precision of the detail and the warmth with which it's delivered. Comparable to the vasectomy anchor example in its use of specific physical comedy to escalate an already dark premise.

jokes.text: I mean, you may have slept with my aunt, but given the circumstances, cheers.
jokes.setup: The two workers realize their families may have crossed paths at Stainsbury's.
jokes.punchline: The cheerful acceptance of 'you may have slept with my aunt' as a reason to toast rather than be horrified is the perfect button on the whole sequence.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Stainsbury sequence. The 'given the circumstances, cheers' — accepting potential familial violation as grounds for bonding rather than disgust — is a lovely dark comedy resolution. The word 'may' is doing quiet comedic work too: not definitely, possibly, but we'll drink to it anyway.

tmdb_overview: The Save Greendale Committee's success is short-lived when the board votes for a corporate sellout, but Pelton, Annie and Abed might find a solution.
insight: Meta storytelling structure sustains 82-point episode across 60 jokes in tight 60-minute format.
